name: Skeaghshee

facts.text: Level 71, 30,000 health, in the Cursed Forest. He takes no damage from magic of any kind (body, cold, energy, heat, matter, spirit): 'Skeaghshee is immune to magic damage!'

Hiberno-English skeagh (Irish sceach, 'whitethorn') + shee (sí, 'fairy'): the fairy thorn. Bot chat glosses it the same way.

In Cath Maige Tuired, Goibniu makes spearheads in three strokes, Luchta the shafts in three cuts and Credne the rivets; Ruadán, son of Bres and the Dagda's daughter, wounds Goibniu with a spear and is killed with it, and his mother's keening is the first in Ireland.
facts.source: Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Mag Tuired)

facts.text: Living Server lore: the smiths of Ardee setting the iron rule beside the thorn rule, and Skeaghshee's weakness to iron.

story:
Every Hibernian farmer knows the rule. A lone whitethorn in a field belongs to the Good Folk, and you do not cut it, plough round it, or hang washing on it; you tie a rag to it for luck and leave it be. Skeaghshee is the reason for the rule. He is the fairy thorn of the court wood, the thorn under which the courts sat to bargain, grown into the shape of a man when the bargain broke beneath him.

He is made of the stuff the fairy courts are made of, and magic of every kind runs off him like rain off a slate: body, cold, energy, heat, matter, spirit, none of it can touch him. Only plain iron and wood and a strong arm will do, and even those he turns a little. The farmers of Ardee still tie rags to the thorns in their fields; now you know why. And when the realm's warriors cut down the fairy thorn of the Cursed Forest, the farmers go out the next morning and tie two.

The smiths of Ardee say the thorn rule is older than the courts, and so is the iron rule that goes with it. When the Tuatha Dé Danann made ready for the second Mag Tuired, their smith Goibniu promised them spearheads that would never miss, and made each one in three strokes of the hammer; Luchta the wright cut the shafts in three cuts, and Credne the brazier made the rivets and cast them into the sockets. The Fomorians sent Ruadán, son of Bres and of the Dagda's daughter, to spy on the smiths. He took up one of the new spears and wounded Goibniu with it. Goibniu drew the spear out of his own body, threw it back and killed him, and Ruadán's mother came to the field and keened him, the first keening ever heard in the land.

The smiths tell that tale over Skeaghshee for its first half, not its last. Plain iron in a smith's hand did what was needed the night the Tuatha went to war, and the thorn of the court wood keeps the rule that makes such iron needful. Magic of the courts' kind runs off him because he grew in the courts' shade. Iron was never theirs, and so it bites, though not as deep as it would bite a man, because he was a tree first.
legend: Spells do nothing to him at all, so this is a melee fight: bring every sword in the realm and leave the casters to heal and strengthen the fighters. Archers and other physical damage still work. And leave the thorn trees alone, the old hibs say. Melee and archers only; casters heal and chant. Superstition: cut the thorn and tie two rags the next morning, or your luck goes for a year. Nicknames: 'the thorn', 'old rag-tree'. Archers love this fight; casters hate it. Shields still help against him; the twenty-in-a-hundred of every blow he turns is the thorn remembering it was wood.

loremasterTopic.text: The fairy thorn, grown into a man. Fairy magic runs off him like rain. Only iron, wood and a strong arm will do.

bookPage: From Derbáil of Ardee's list: grandmother said every farmer in Hibernia keeps the thorn rule, and the reason is in the Cursed Forest. The courts sat under a whitethorn to bargain, and when the bargain broke under it the thorn stood up and walked. No magic touches him; he is made of fairy stuff. Only iron. When the realm's warriors cut him down, she said, you go out the next morning and tie two rags to the nearest thorn instead of one. One for luck, and one by way of apology, because a thorn is a thorn whatever it has become.
